skills.name: Mushroom and yeast: structure, mode of life and importance of fungi

note.text:
Mushroom: the part above ground is the fruiting body: a stalk (stipe) and a cap (pileus) with gills underneath, where spores are made. Most of the mushroom is an underground mycelium feeding saprophytically on dead matter.
Yeast: single oval cells; reproduces by budding. It respires anaerobically in sugar solution (fermentation): glucose → ethanol (alcohol) + carbon dioxide + energy.
Importance of fungi:
• Useful: food (mushrooms), yeast in bread (CO₂ makes dough rise) and in brewing; antibiotics (penicillin from Penicillium); decomposers that recycle nutrients.
• Harmful: diseases of people (ringworm, athlete's foot, thrush), of crops (black pod of cocoa, maize smut), food spoilage, and poisonous mushrooms.

sections.heading: The mushroom
sections.text:
What we call a mushroom is only the fruiting body. It has a stalk and a cap; under the cap are thin gills where millions of spores form and drop into the wind.
The main body of the fungus is a mycelium of hyphae spread through the soil or rotting wood, feeding on dead matter as a saprophyte.

sections.heading: Yeast
sections.text:
Yeast is a single-celled fungus with oval cells. It reproduces by budding: a small bud grows out and breaks off.
In sugar solution without oxygen it ferments: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide + energy.
Bakers use the carbon dioxide to make dough rise; brewers and palm wine tappers rely on the alcohol.

sections.heading: Friends and foes
sections.text:
Useful fungi: edible mushrooms; yeast for bread and fermentation; Penicillium, which gives the antibiotic penicillin; decomposers that recycle nutrients.
Harmful fungi: ringworm, athlete's foot and thrush in people; black pod of cocoa and smuts of maize; moulds that spoil food; poisonous mushrooms.

reproduction by a small outgrowth that breaks off
anaerobic respiration of sugar by yeast

examples: Black pod: fungal disease of cocoa

mistake.wrong: Yeast makes bread rise by producing oxygen
mistake.right: Yeast makes bread rise by producing carbon dioxide
mistake.why: Fermentation releases carbon dioxide, which is trapped in the dough.

worked_example.problem: Explain why yeast makes bread dough rise.
steps: Yeast respires the sugar in the dough.
The gas bubbles are trapped in the dough, so it swells; baking kills the yeast and sets the bread.
worked_example.answer: Carbon dioxide from yeast respiration is trapped in the dough

example: Cap, gills and stalk above ground; mycelium below

pick.q: Which disease of cocoa in Cameroon is caused by a fungus?
e: Malaria is a human disease caused by a protoctist.
Cholera is a bacterial human disease.
Measles is a viral human disease.

pick.q: How do fungi help keep soils fertile?
pick.r: As decomposers they break down dead matter and release nutrients
w: They fix nitrogen in root nodules
e: Most fungi do not eat insects.

pick.q: Where are the spores of a mushroom produced?
pick.r: on the gills under the cap
e: The stalk holds the cap up.
Spores form above ground on the gills.
pick.y: Gills release spores into the air.

pick.q: Most of a mushroom's body is…
e: The cap is only the fruiting body.
Gills are only part of the cap.
pick.y: The visible part is just for spreading spores.
A small bud grows from the parent cell and breaks off.

pick.q: What are the products of fermentation by yeast?
e: Those are not products of fermentation.

pick.q: Which gas makes bread dough rise?
e: Yeast uses oxygen if available but does not release it.
pick.y: Yeast releases CO₂ that is trapped in the dough.

pick.q: Why is palm wine sweet when freshly tapped but becomes alcoholic after a day?
pick.r: Yeasts ferment its sugar into alcohol
w: The sun turns sugar into alcohol
Bacteria add alcohol from the air
e: Yeasts, not added alcohol, are the cause.
